spacertales-second-shift-record.label: Crew copies
spacertales-second-shift-record.title: The signatures left off the invoice
spacertales-second-shift-record.body:
A repair invoice is written for someone who expects to pay, or someone who hopes to collect. A crew's copy is often written for the next person who has to make the ship work. Those purposes overlap without being identical.

Independent crews keep covering letters, dates, parts lists and accounts of work supplied from wages. Some copies pass from ship to ship. Others remain with a former worker who knows what an unexplained line in the inventory meant. They are not a registry, a union or a substitute for a contract.

A machine can carry a maker's plate, a finance label and somebody else's repair marks. Each names a different part of its history. A later claim may be easier to read if all three are retained.

Copies are not automatically reliable. A signed letter can preserve a mistake as carefully as a fact. Useful records distinguish what the writer saw, what someone told them and what nobody could settle.

Crews tend to remember the person who found the fault. Office accounts tend to remember the part ordered afterwards. A ship's useful history usually needs room for both.

spacertales-sable-margin-history.label: Refits and ownership
spacertales-sable-margin-history.title: A working ship, twice on paper
spacertales-sable-margin-history.body:
A contractor's inventory and a crew's account can describe the same refit with different owners. One records finance and replacement orders. The other records repairs, borrowed fittings and purchases made from wages while those orders were still pending.

The name on the machine tells you its maker. It does not settle which account paid for it, which vessel later carried it or whose work kept it useful between deliveries. A material sample can identify a present product without proving the origin of an old batch.

Ship sales add another layer. Names change, offices move and workers take their copies to new berths. A plate number may outlast the address on the original invoice.

A receiving clerk can correct a cargo description. That does not give the clerk authority to decide a contract. Brokers who ask for a clean summary are sometimes asking for a conclusion the papers cannot supply.

Independent crews keep rough copies because a tidy account written afterwards can be much more confident than the people who did the job.

spacertales-short-return-history.label: Fitting a sickbay
spacertales-short-return-history.title: A place kept clear
spacertales-short-return-history.body:
A sickbay refit changes the loading plan before it changes anyone's health. The bed needs a place, the patient needs a way to reach it, and another crew member needs room to work beside them. A crate waiting to be moved is still in that room.

Halewright fitting correspondence separates those needs from the equipment bill. A bed supplied is not necessarily a bed accessible. A drawer supplied is not necessarily a drawer stocked. Power and air remain part of the room's ordinary work.

Care has records of its own: watch times, supplies brought to the patient and the people who could stay while someone else did the ship's other jobs. The Vigil-2 can observe. It cannot supply that watch or do the treating.

Private crew letters may be worth retaining without being suitable for a clinical conclusion. An account of a return to dock cannot, by itself, identify an injury or establish which treatment worked.

Equipment can be sold separately when a ship changes hands. Crews sometimes keep the fitting and watch accounts together because those records explain what an inventory alone leaves out.

spacertales-double-freight-claim.title: One shipment, two owners
spacertales-double-freight-claim.text: Two former contractors have asked the receiving desk at [place] about the same Sable Margin shipment. [person:spacertales-neri-vale] is checking an ambiguous cargo description before circulating any correction. A crew covering letter gives a third account of repairs and purchases from wages. The desk has a description to compare; it has no ownership verdict.
mention: The Sable Margin file at [place] has two contractors and a crew account. One cargo description needs checking first.
Two contractors and a crew letter, all about the same Sable Margin cargo at [place]. The description gets checked before anything else.

spacertales-second-shift-correction.title: The names in the margin
spacertales-second-shift-correction.text: At [place], receiving clerk [person:spacertales-neri-vale] has circulated a correction to the Sable Margin freight account after an independent crew supplied a present-day Rivetline can for comparison with the old item description. Vale says the example clarified the terminology, not ownership. The revised account distinguishes what the documents establish from what their claimants want them to establish. Former crew say it is a useful start.
mention: [person:spacertales-neri-vale]'s corrected the Sable Margin freight account. A can can settle a name. Ownership takes more paper.
[person:spacertales-neri-vale] corrected the Sable Margin account. The can cleared up a word, not who owns what.

spacertales-yard-signatures-news.title: The sample was not the proof
spacertales-yard-signatures-news.text: At [place], an addendum to the Sable Margin papers distinguishes a material sample from evidence of where it was made. Clerk [person:spacertales-neri-vale] says a recent Rivetline ingot example helped read the old catalogue, but proves nothing about a historical refit. Former workers have asked for their signed repair letters to be considered separately. A broker says separate evidence makes the file harder to summarise.
mention: The Sable Margin sample showed what an ingot was. Didn't prove who made the old one. Workers still have their letters.
That ingot sample explained the old catalogue. It didn't say who made the Sable Margin's metal. The workers' letters stand on their own.

spacertales-verdemorrow-meal-record.title: The meal had names
spacertales-verdemorrow-meal-record.text: At [place], Verdemorrow's archive has appended a crew account to the often-reprinted Sable Margin galley photograph. The account names the people who tended the crop and prepared the meal. It makes no claim about yield, growing conditions or the ownership of equipment. A former contractor has objected that the additional caption distracts from its provision programme. The archivist says it explains who provided supper.
mention: Verdemorrow's put the crew names under the old galley photo. Contractor preferred its own caption.
The old galley photo has the crew's names under it now. The contractor isn't pleased; supper was the crew's doing.

spacertales-halewright-watch-record.title: The watch was people
spacertales-halewright-watch-record.text: At [place], Halewright has added a watchkeeper's letter to the Short Return fitting correspondence. The letter distinguishes the supplied bed and monitor from the crew who kept the patient company and did the care work. The archive says no clinical conclusion can be drawn from the surviving account. A former watchkeeper says the point was to preserve the names, not sell another bed.
mention: Halewright's kept the Short Return watch letter. The equipment got the invoice. The people finally got their names.
The Short Return letter is kept with the names of the people who sat the watch. The bed and monitor were only the equipment.

spacertales-mixed-makers-spares.title: Common parts, separate promises
text: Equipment brokers at [place] are being asked for one clear list of stores and connections for mixed plants. Fennmark, Tolvane, Lixivar and Oxsmith dealers each describe their own products. Operators say four leaflets can still leave one gap. A local broker is gathering the descriptions before returning a proposed bill.

Operators of mixed plants at [place] want brokers to give them one clear list of stores and connections. Fennmark, Tolvane, Lixivar and Oxsmith dealers each describe only their own machines, and four leaflets, operators say, can still leave one gap. A local broker is collecting the descriptions before sending back a proposed bill.
mention: Four makers can write four correct leaflets and still leave you guessing what joins the machines.
Each maker's leaflet is right about its own machine. Put four together and there's still a hole where the connections go.

spacertales-yard-worker-loss.title: The last repair note
text: At [place], a small salvage contractor is disputing payment to a worker whose repair notes were used after she left its payroll. Crew say the notes kept a refit moving when replacement equipment was delayed. Management says the worker supplied knowledge, not a part with a listed value. Rivetline dealers have declined to price the notes. The worker says pricing them was not the original question.

A worker's repair notes kept a refit going at [place] after she had left a small salvage contractor's payroll, and now she wants paying. Crew say the notes carried the work through delayed replacement equipment. Management says she supplied knowledge, not a part with a listed value. Rivetline dealers will not price the notes; the worker says price was never her question.
mention: A contractor used a worker's repair notes, then said knowledge wasn't a payable part. She says she asked for wages.
They used her repair notes after she'd gone, then said notes aren't a part. She only asked for wages.

spacertales-warehouse-watch-rumour.title: A light on the closed shelf
text: At [place], a freight clerk has dismissed reports of a signal light seen among boxed control equipment in a closed stores aisle. The stock was disconnected and the watch camera recorded only the aisle entrance. Asterel says it cannot diagnose a story without the actual hardware. Night staff have requested another lamp for the aisle. Management is reviewing whether poor lighting counts as an equipment fault.

Reports of a signal light among boxed control equipment in a closed stores aisle at [place] have been dismissed by a freight clerk. The stock was disconnected, and the watch camera covered only the aisle entrance. Without the hardware itself, Asterel says, it cannot diagnose a story. Night staff want another lamp; management is considering whether poor lighting counts as an equipment fault.
mention: Night crew saw a light in the boxed Asterel stock. Service wants the board. Management wants fewer lamps.
A light in a crate of disconnected Asterel gear. The night crew asked for another lamp, not an exorcist.

spacertales-ledger-freight-notice.title: A description to check
text: The receiving desk at [place] is asking independent crews for help reading an old equipment description. A current Rivetline D20 can would make a useful comparison. The desk says it wants an example, not the can itself, and will send the questions by correspondence. No ownership claim will be settled by the comparison.

Independent crews are being asked to help the receiving desk at [place] read an old equipment description, and a current Rivetline D20 can would be a useful comparison. The desk wants an example, not the can, and will send its questions by correspondence. The comparison will settle no ownership claim.
mention: The receiving desk at [place] wants a D20 comparison. You keep the can. They keep the paperwork.
Got a D20 can? The receiving desk at [place] wants to compare it, not keep it.

spacertales-asterel-service-result.title: The number kept the letter
spacertales-asterel-service-result.text: The Asterel desk at [place] has attached the old watchkeeper's covering letter to the Sable Margin receiving file. A plate number connected the record through the ship's changed names. The copy preserves a repair account separately from the office's replacement note. It extends no warranty and tests no present board.
mention: Asterel's plate number kept the letter with the receiving file. The new module isn't carrying an old warranty.
Asterel matched the old letter by plate number. It's on file; no warranty came with it.

spacertales-mixed-plant-closed.title: No order placed
spacertales-mixed-plant-closed.text: The mixed-plant quotation at [place] has closed without an order. [person:spacertales-orra-pell] retained the four useful makers' descriptions and returned the incomplete bill. Matching finish was offered in place of the missing connections. The customer's ships have gained no equipment or joint service agreement through this correspondence.
mention: The mixed-plant bill closed with no sale. Four useful leaflets survived; matching paint didn't fill the gap.
No sale on that mixed-plant bill. The leaflets were useful; matching paint couldn't stand in for the joints.

spacertales-pump-accounts-kept.title: Two accounts, no location
spacertales-pump-accounts-kept.text: Alembrine's correspondence desk at [place] has retained both accounts of the bottle sent over a borrowed pump. A current product comparison clarified the label, not the old destination. The desk will not combine the letters into a reconciled ending. The pump's owner is still asking for a location.
mention: Alembrine kept both pump letters at [place]. Better filing hasn't brought the pump back.
Both pump letters are on file at [place]. Still no pump.

spacertales-drawings-kept.title: Both sheets retained
spacertales-drawings-kept.text: The drawing correspondence forwarded through [place] has closed with both historical sheets retained. The old sales drawing and the crew's later drawing describe different stages of the ship's life. The receiving copy contains letters, not a working schematic. Nobody's ship is being rebuilt to settle an argument over paper.
mention: Both drawings stayed in the file at [place]. Keeping a ship's history doesn't mean building it twice.
The old drawing and the crew's drawing are both kept at [place]. Nobody's rebuilding a ship to settle it.

spacertales-loading-caption-corrected.title: The loading had a worker
spacertales-loading-caption-corrected.text: Slingwright's letters desk at [place] has filed a corrected caption beside the worker's signed account. The RM-1 did its job with accepted stock; a person supplied that stock. The photograph's description now keeps those jobs separate. The disputed loading fee remains unpaid in the account. No payment or new batch followed the correction.
mention: Slingwright's caption finally counts the loading. The fee in that old account is still disputed.
The Slingwright caption mentions the loader now. The loading fee is another matter.

line: The second-shift ledger names the worker before the machine. First catalogue I've read that knew what kept a ship going.
In the second-shift ledger, the people come before the parts. That's the right order.
Read the second-shift ledger: names first, machines after. Somebody understood ships.
[person:spacertales-neri-vale]'s letters don't decide who owns the Sable Margin's parts. They make it harder to forget who repaired them.
[person:spacertales-neri-vale] isn't ruling on who owns the Sable Margin's parts. The letters just keep the repairers on the record.
Those letters from [person:spacertales-neri-vale] settle nothing about ownership. They do remember who did the repairs.
Two owners claimed the same stores. I'd settle for both paying the same repair bill.
Two people claiming the same stores. I'd like to see them both claim the repair bill.
Everyone owns the stores until the repair invoice arrives.
Leave a copy of the repair note with somebody who leaves the ship. Records get lonely when there's only one.
Give a copy of the repair notes to someone leaving the ship. A record kept in one place is half lost.
Always send a copy of the repair note off with someone who's leaving. One copy is no copy.
Old invoices belong with this ship's papers. Somebody may eventually ask which parts were only borrowed.
Keep the old invoices with the ship's papers. One day somebody will ask what was only on loan.
I'd hang on to those old invoices. Somebody always turns up asking which parts weren't really ours.
Asterel store clerk saw a light in a disconnected crate. Might've been a reflection. She wants a second lamp before finding out.
That Asterel clerk saw a light where nothing was plugged in. Probably a reflection. She still wants a second lamp first.
A light in a dead crate, the night clerk says. Whatever it was, she's asking for better lighting before she looks again.
That Short Return letter thanked the people who stayed on watch. The monitor had its job; staying awake beside someone was theirs.
The Short Return letter remembers who stayed awake with the patient. The monitor did its job; the people did theirs.
What I liked about the Short Return letter: it thanks the people on watch, not the equipment.
If the only record of a job belongs to the person who didn't do it, whose history is it?
If the only record of the work is held by someone who didn't do it, whose story does it tell?
Whose history is it, when the paperwork belongs to the one person who wasn't there?

spacertales-ledger-history.text: Crews keep copies of repair letters because an invoice can name the part without naming the person who kept it working. A useful copy keeps the date, the signature and the uncertainty.

spacertales-short-return-ending.text: Sickbay correspondence can preserve fitting plans and care work without proving a medical outcome. A return to dock is a crew account, not a treatment result.

spacertales-sable-margin-history-tip.text: Two inventories can describe the same refit and disagree about who paid. A maker's plate identifies equipment; it does not decide which account owns it.
